# Plan: RMI distribution (Client → Middleware → Flights/Cars/Rooms RMs), customers held in the Middleware

## Context
The template is a single-process RMI server. The spec (RMI task, points 1–4) asks for:
1. A **Middleware** that implements the same interface as the RM, is given the RM hosts at startup, and is the only server the client talks to.
2. Three RMs (Flights, Cars, Rooms). They can all run the unchanged `ResourceManager` code; the Middleware just sends each type's calls to the matching RM.
3. A decision on where customers live. **You chose the Middleware**, so the Middleware "becomes a type of ResourceManager".
4. A working `bundle`.

The client source must not change. `IResourceManager` (the only thing in `RMIInterface.jar`) also stays as it is.

## Core design problem, and the fix
`ResourceManager.reserveItem` expects the customer and the item to be in the **same** `m_data` map. Once customers live in the Middleware and items live in the RMs, the Middleware needs an RM operation that atomically checks availability, decrements the count and returns the price. It also needs the inverse, to cancel reservations. The public interface has neither.

The fix is a new server-internal remote interface, `Server/Interface/IResourceManagerInternal.java`, which extends `IResourceManager` and adds:
- `int reserveResource(String key)`: under `synchronized(m_data)`, if the item exists and `count > 0`, it does `count--` and `reserved++` and returns the price. Otherwise it returns `-1`.
- `boolean unreserveResource(String key, int n)`: under `synchronized(m_data)`, it does `count += n` and `reserved -= n`. This is used by deleteCustomer and by bundle rollback.

Keeping these off `IResourceManager` means `RMIInterface.jar` and the client stay untouched.

## Portion 1: RM side (`Server/Common/ResourceManager.java`)
- Change it to `implements IResourceManagerInternal` and add the two methods above. Build them on the existing `readData`/`writeData`, with the whole check-and-update wrapped in `synchronized(m_data)` (the lock is reentrant) so two concurrent reservations can't both take the last seat.
- No other changes. The RM's existing customer methods simply go unused in the distributed setup.
- `RMIResourceManager.java` stays as it is. The stub `UnicastRemoteObject.exportObject` generates implements every remote interface of the object, so the Middleware can cast the lookup result to `IResourceManagerInternal`.

## Portion 2: Middleware (`Server/RMI/RMIMiddleware.java`, new)
`public class RMIMiddleware extends ResourceManager`. Extending `ResourceManager` means it inherits the local `m_data` customer store, `newCustomer()`, `newCustomer(int)` and `queryCustomerInfo`, all unchanged.

**Startup (`main(flightsHost, carsHost, roomsHost)`):**
- Connect to `group_47_Flights`, `group_47_Cars` and `group_47_Rooms` on the given hosts. Use a retry loop copied from `Client/Client/RMIClient.connectServer`: `LocateRegistry.getRegistry(host, 1099).lookup(...)`, retrying on `NotBoundException`/`RemoteException` every 500 ms.
- Export itself and bind as `group_47_Middleware`, reusing the create-or-get registry code and the shutdown hook from `RMIResourceManager.main`.

**Pure forwarding** (one line per method): the `add*`, `delete{Flight,Cars,Rooms}`, `query*` and `query*Price` methods go to `m_flightsRM`, `m_carsRM` or `m_roomsRM`.

**Customer-aware operations** (overridden). Each takes a per-customer lock (`ConcurrentHashMap<Integer,Object>`), so operations on the same customer are serialized and different customers run in parallel:
- `reserveFlight/Car/Room`: a shared helper `reserveItem(cid, rm, key, location)` checks that the customer exists locally, calls `rm.reserveResource(key)`, and on a price ≥ 0 calls `customer.reserve(key, location, price)` and `writeData`. Keys come from the existing `Flight.getKey` / `Car.getKey` / `Room.getKey`.

- [RMIMiddleware.java](Template/Server/Server/RMI/RMIMiddleware.java) (new): stores customers locally and passes flight, car and room calls to the matching server. Reserve, delete-customer and bundle lock per customer. Bundle is all-or-nothing and gives back anything already taken if a step fails.

content.text:
I've wrapped `deleteItem` in `synchronized(m_data)`, and the server compiles. I haven't rerun the end-to-end tests after this change; I can if you'd like.

## 1. The resource manager fix, in simpler terms

When the Middleware looks up a server, RMI sends it a "remote control" object (the stub). The stub offers every remote interface the real server's class implements.

- **First version:** `ResourceManager` implemented `IResourceManagerInternal`. Both `RMIResourceManager` and `RMIMiddleware` are built on `ResourceManager`, so both inherited it.
- **Why that broke the client:** the Middleware's stub therefore offered `IResourceManagerInternal` too. When the client received that stub, Java tried to load the class for every interface on it. The client only has `IResourceManager` (it's the only class in `RMIInterface.jar`), so loading failed and the client kept retrying.
- **The fix:** declare `IResourceManagerInternal` only on `RMIResourceManager`. The two methods still live in `ResourceManager`, so no code is duplicated. Now the three item servers expose the internal methods to the Middleware, and the Middleware exposes only `IResourceManager` to the client.

## 2. The race

`DeleteFlight` did take a lock, but only for each small step, not for the whole operation. `readData` and `removeData` each lock `m_data` on their own and release it when they return. `deleteItem` does:

1. `readData(key)`: lock, copy the flight, unlock
2. check that `reserved == 0`
3. `removeData(key)`: lock, remove, unlock

Between steps 1 and 3 the lock is free, so a reservation can run in that gap:

| Time | Thread A: `DeleteFlight,10` | Thread B: `ReserveFlight,1,10` |
|---|---|---|
| t1 | reads flight 10: reserved = 0 | |
| t2 | | `reserveResource`: reserved becomes 1, seat taken |
| t3 | checks its copy: reserved is 0, so it deletes | |
| t4 | removes flight 10 | |

At the end, customer 1's bill shows a seat on a flight that no longer exists. Deleting customer 1 later would try to give that seat back and fail, because the flight is gone.

This is a "check-then-act" race. The lock protected each read and write, but not the check and the action together.

**How the fix closes it:** `deleteItem` now holds `synchronized(m_data)` for the whole read, check and remove. `reserveResource` locks the same object, so the two can no longer interleave. The one that runs second sees the other's result: either the flight is gone and the reservation fails, or `reserved` is 1 and the delete is refused.

Java locks are reentrant, so the `readData` and `removeData` calls inside the block re-enter the lock this thread already holds instead of deadlocking.

content.text: so for the resource manager fix, you made it a class method instead of an interface method so that all of the classes can take the same interface without issue?

Close, but two details differ:

1. **They're still ordinary instance methods.** "Class method" in Java usually means `static`, and they aren't. `reserveResource` and `unreserveResource` are regular public methods on `ResourceManager`, just as before. Only one line moved: `implements IResourceManagerInternal` now sits on `RMIResourceManager` instead of `ResourceManager`.

2. **The classes now expose *different* interfaces, and that's the point:**

| Class | Has the methods? | Declares which interface? | Its stub exposes |
|---|---|---|---|
| `ResourceManager` | yes (defines them) | `IResourceManager` | (not exported) |
| `RMIResourceManager` | yes (inherited) | `IResourceManagerInternal` | `IResourceManagerInternal` (which includes `IResourceManager`) |
| `RMIMiddleware` | yes (inherited, but unused) | only `IResourceManager`, inherited | `IResourceManager` only |

RMI decides what a stub offers from the interfaces a class *declares*, not from the methods it happens to have. `RMIMiddleware` does contain `reserveResource`, but because it never declares `IResourceManagerInternal`, that method isn't part of its stub and can't be called remotely. So the client gets a stub it can load, and the Middleware gets stubs with the extra methods it needs.

Put simply: the code for the methods is shared by all three classes, and the "remotely callable" label is added only to the item servers.
i am not sure i understand what the original issue was now. if we want all three classes to have these methods, why wouldn't we want them to have the same interface?

We don't actually want all three to *expose* these methods. It only looks that way because the code is shared.

**Who needs to call `reserveResource`?** Only the Middleware, and only on the three item servers (Flights, Cars, Rooms). Nobody ever calls it on the Middleware: the client has no command for it and doesn't know it exists.

**Why does the Middleware have the methods at all?** It's a side effect. `RMIMiddleware extends ResourceManager` so it can reuse the customer storage (`m_data`, `newCustomer`, `queryCustomerInfo`). Inheriting from `ResourceManager` brings every method along, including `reserveResource`. The Middleware simply never uses it.

**The original issue:**
1. Putting `implements IResourceManagerInternal` on `ResourceManager` meant every subclass inherited that interface, including `RMIMiddleware`.
2. So the Middleware's stub (what RMI sends the client) said: "I implement `IResourceManager` **and** `IResourceManagerInternal`."
3. When the client receives a stub, Java must load the class file for **every** interface listed on it.
4. The client only has `RMIInterface.jar`, which contains `IResourceManager` and nothing else. Loading `IResourceManagerInternal` failed, and the client couldn't connect.

**Why not just give all three the same interface and add `IResourceManagerInternal` to the jar?** That would also work, but it has two downsides:
- `RMIInterface.jar` is the client-facing contract, and we'd be changing it for something the client never uses.
- It would let a client call `unreserveResource("flight-10", 100)` directly on the Middleware and create 100 seats out of nothing. That is an internal operation that should stay internal.

So the aim isn't "all three classes share the methods". It's "the Middleware can call these methods on the item servers, and the client never sees them". Declaring the interface only on `RMIResourceManager` does that: the code is shared through inheritance, and the remote-access label goes only on the servers that need it.

What it calls are the item servers' versions, through their stubs (`m_flightsRM.reserveResource(...)`). Those stubs do carry `IResourceManagerInternal`, because `RMIResourceManager` declares it. content.text:
`RMIResourceManager` doesn't sit between the client and the Middleware. It sits **behind** the Middleware. It's the program each of the three item servers runs. A request goes Client → Middleware → `RMIResourceManager`, never the other way round.

## Runtime flow: 5 processes, possibly on 4 machines

```
 ┌──────────────────────┐
 │ Client  (RMIClient)  │   has only RMIInterface.jar (IResourceManager)
 └──────────┬───────────┘
            │ RMI calls on IResourceManager
            │ e.g. reserveFlight(1, 10), bundle(...), queryCustomer(1)
            ▼
 ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Middleware process  (java Server.RMI.RMIMiddleware ...)     │
 │   registry name: group_47_Middleware                        │
 │                                                             │
 │   customers live HERE (its own m_data):                     │
 │     "customer-1" → bill: flight-10 $100, car-montreal $50   │
 │                                                             │
 │   add/query/delete flight → forward to Flights              │
 │   reserveFlight → reserveResource on Flights, then update   │
 │                   the customer's bill locally               │
 └───────┬───────────────────────┬───────────────────────┬─────┘
         │ RMI calls on IResourceManagerInternal         │
         │ addFlight, queryFlight, reserveResource,      │
         │ unreserveResource, ...                        │
         ▼                       ▼                       ▼
 ┌────────────────┐     ┌────────────────┐     ┌────────────────┐
 │ Flights process│     │ Cars process   │     │ Rooms process  │
 │ RMIResource-   │     │ RMIResource-   │     │ RMIResource-   │
 │ Manager        │     │ Manager        │     │ Manager        │
 │ "Flights"      │     │ "Cars"         │     │ "Rooms"        │
 │                │     │                │     │                │
 │ m_data:        │     │ m_data:        │     │ m_data:        │
 │  flight-10     │     │  car-montreal  │     │  room-montreal │
 │  flight-11     │     │                │     │                │
 └────────────────┘     └────────────────┘     └────────────────┘
```

Example: `ReserveFlight,1,10`:
1. The client calls `middleware.reserveFlight(1, 10)`.
2. The Middleware locks customer 1 and checks that customer 1 exists in its own `m_data`.
3. The Middleware calls `flightsRM.reserveResource("flight-10")`. Flights decrements the seat count and returns `$100`.
4. The Middleware adds `flight-10 $100` to customer 1's bill and returns `true` to the client.

## Class structure: where the code lives

```
                IResourceManager            (in RMIInterface.jar; the client sees this)
                       ▲
                       │ extends
          IResourceManagerInternal          (server-only: + reserveResource, unreserveResource)

 ResourceManager  implements IResourceManager
   • all the business logic: m_data, add/query/delete, customers,
     reserveResource, unreserveResource
   • no RMI code at all
        ▲                                   ▲
        │ extends                           │ extends
 RMIResourceManager                   RMIMiddleware
   implements IResourceManagerInternal   (implements only IResourceManager, inherited)
   • adds main(): export + bind          • adds main(): connect to the 3 RMs, export + bind
   • run 3 times: Flights/Cars/Rooms     • overrides flight/car/room methods to forward,
                                         • overrides reserve/deleteCustomer/bundle
```

## So what is `RMIResourceManager` for?

`ResourceManager` is plain Java logic with no networking. `RMIResourceManager` is the thin wrapper that turns that logic into a network server. It adds two things:
1. **`main()`**: creates the object, exports it with `UnicastRemoteObject`, and binds it in the registry under `group_47_Flights` (or `Cars`, or `Rooms`).
2. **`implements IResourceManagerInternal`**: lets the Middleware call the reservation methods remotely.

The same class runs three times with a different name argument. Each copy only ever receives its own type of item, because the Middleware sends flight calls only to Flights, car calls only to Cars, and so on.

`RMIMiddleware` is the same kind of wrapper. It also builds on `ResourceManager`, but it replaces the flight, car and room methods so they forward to the item servers, and it keeps the customer methods local.

so the resourcemanager is like a service method (where the actual logic takes place), rmiresourcemanager does the networking and the middleware gives server (resource managers) access to the clients. is that correct?

Yes, that's essentially right. Three refinements:

1. **`ResourceManager` is a service class, not a method.** Think of it as the service layer: every operation's logic lives there (add, query, delete, the reserve bookkeeping, customer bills), with no networking code.

2. **`RMIResourceManager` does the networking, and only a little of it.** Its `main()` publishes a `ResourceManager` on the network, and it declares the internal interface. RMI itself does the actual sending of messages; you never write socket code in this part.

3. **The Middleware does more than pass requests through.** It is:
   - **the single entry point.** Clients only ever talk to the Middleware and never contact the item servers directly. Clients don't even know those servers exist.
   - **a router.** Flight calls go to Flights, car calls to Cars, room calls to Rooms.
   - **a resource manager in its own right, for customers.** It stores the customers and coordinates the operations that involve both a customer and an item: reserve, delete customer, and bundle with its rollback.

The spec's wording for the Middleware fits your picture: because customers live there, it "becomes a type of ResourceManager".

In one line: **the client talks to the Middleware (routing plus customers), which talks to three `RMIResourceManager` servers (the network wrapper), each running `ResourceManager` logic (the service layer).**

the client sends its request to the middleware, the middleware routes the request to the correct rmi resource manager, who will then send the request to the service class, get a response and then send it back up the chain. is this correct?

Close. The one inaccurate part is "the RMI resource manager sends the request to the service class". No hand-off happens there, because they are the same object.

`RMIResourceManager extends ResourceManager`, so each item server holds exactly **one** object, and that object *is* a `ResourceManager`. When the Middleware calls `flightsRM.queryFlight(10)`:

1. The Middleware's stub turns the call into a network message and sends it to the Flights process.
2. RMI's runtime in the Flights process receives the message and calls `queryFlight(10)` directly on that one object. That method is the inherited `ResourceManager` code; `RMIResourceManager` doesn't touch the request.
3. The return value travels back the same way: Flights → Middleware → client.

`RMIResourceManager`'s code (`main()`) runs only once, at startup, to publish the object. After that, RMI calls the business logic directly.

Two more details on the Middleware step, because not every request is simply routed:

| Request type | What the Middleware does |
|---|---|
| Flight/car/room add, query, delete | Forwards one call to the right item server and returns its answer |
| `AddCustomer`, `QueryCustomer` | Handles it itself; no item server is involved |
| `Reserve*` | Checks the customer locally, calls `reserveResource` on the item server, then updates the customer's bill locally |
| `DeleteCustomer` | Calls `unreserveResource` on each server the customer has reservations with, then deletes the customer locally |
| `Bundle` | Calls `reserveResource` several times, possibly on all three servers, and rolls back if any step fails |

Corrected chain: **Client → Middleware (routes, or handles customer work itself) → item server, where RMI calls the `ResourceManager` logic directly → the response comes back the same path.**

content.text:
Each server does get a full copy of every method, but each one only ever uses its own slice. That's a deliberate simplification the spec allows: *"you can keep only one implementation providing the entire interface – the Middleware will only call the flight-methods on the flight ResourceManager."*

## What each process actually uses

| Process | Code it has | Code it actually uses | What ends up in its `m_data` |
|---|---|---|---|
| Flights | all of `ResourceManager` | `addFlight`, `queryFlight`, `deleteFlight`, `reserveResource`/`unreserveResource` on `flight-*` keys | only `flight-*` items |
| Cars | all of it | the car methods | only `car-*` items |
| Rooms | all of it | the room methods | only `room-*` items |
| Middleware | all of it (inherited) | `newCustomer`, `queryCustomerInfo`, `readData`/`writeData`; it replaces the rest with forwarding code | only `customer-*` records |

The car methods in the Flights process are harmless dead weight. Nobody calls them, so the Flights map never contains a car.

## Why one class instead of four

1. **Less code, and no duplication.** Flights, cars and rooms work identically. They differ only in the key format (`flight-10` vs. `car-montreal`), and the shared helpers (`deleteItem`, `queryNum`, `queryPrice`, `reserveResource`) already work for any key. Splitting would mean three near-identical classes.
2. **The Middleware reuses it.** Because customers live in the Middleware, `RMIMiddleware` inherits the customer storage and methods (`newCustomer`, `queryCustomerInfo`) instead of reimplementing them.
3. **It has no networking code, so the TCP part can reuse it too.** For the sockets version, the TCP server will receive a message and call the same `ResourceManager` methods. Only the wrapper changes (RMI's `main()` becomes a socket listener). That's the reason for keeping business logic separate from networking.

## The alternative

You could split it into `FlightResourceManager`, `CarResourceManager`, `RoomResourceManager` and `CustomerManager`, each with only its own methods. That's cleaner in the sense that each server only has what it needs. The costs are more code, some duplication, and the Middleware would still need something implementing the whole `IResourceManager` for the client.

For this assignment, the single shared class is the standard, spec-sanctioned choice. If you'd rather have the split version, for the report or to match your partner's design, I can do that refactor.

content.text: so each rmi resource manager extends the big resource manager class and picks and chooses what it wants to use, making each rmi resource manager its own service class that interacts with only the middleware?

Almost. Two corrections:

1. **There is one `RMIResourceManager` class, run as three separate processes.** There aren't three different subclasses. You start the same class three times with different name arguments:
   ```
   java Server.RMI.RMIResourceManager Flights
   java Server.RMI.RMIResourceManager Cars
   java Server.RMI.RMIResourceManager Rooms
   ```
   Each run creates one object with its own separate `m_data`, bound under its own name (`group_47_Flights`, and so on). All three copies have identical code; the name is the only difference.

2. **The item servers don't pick and choose; the Middleware does.** Nothing in `RMIResourceManager` says "I'm Flights, so reject car requests". Every copy would accept any call. It's the Middleware that only ever calls flight methods on the Flights copy, car methods on the Cars copy, and room methods on the Rooms copy. Each server therefore ends up holding only one type of data, because that's all it's ever asked to store.

The last part of your statement is right: **only the Middleware talks to them.** The client never contacts an item server directly; it doesn't even know their names or hosts. The Middleware is given those hosts on its command line.

Corrected version: **one `RMIResourceManager` class (the full `ResourceManager` logic plus RMI startup) runs as three independent servers. The Middleware decides which server gets which calls, so each one acts as a single-type service, and the Middleware is its only caller.**

content.text:
Yes, you have it right. Java lets an interface method be satisfied by a method the class **inherits**, not only by one it writes itself.

`RMIResourceManager` doesn't define `reserveResource` or `unreserveResource`. When it declares `implements IResourceManagerInternal`, the compiler checks every method the interface requires, looking in `RMIResourceManager` and all its superclasses. It finds both methods in `ResourceManager`:

- [ResourceManager.java:152](Template/Server/Server/Common/ResourceManager.java#L152): `public int reserveResource(String key) throws RemoteException`
- [ResourceManager.java:176](Template/Server/Server/Common/ResourceManager.java#L176): `public boolean unreserveResource(String key, int count) throws RemoteException`

These match the declarations in [IResourceManagerInternal.java:19-29](Template/Server/Server/Interface/IResourceManagerInternal.java#L19-L29) exactly: same name, parameter types and return type, both `public`, and they throw nothing beyond `RemoteException`. So the requirement is met and it compiles. The earlier `make` succeeded, which confirms it.

This isn't new to the internal interface. It's how `RMIResourceManager` satisfied `IResourceManager` all along. The template's `RMIResourceManager` never defined `addFlight`, `queryFlight` and the rest; those were always inherited from `ResourceManager` too.

The inherited method has to be `public` with a matching signature. If `reserveResource` were `protected`, or took an `int` instead of a `String`, the compiler would reject `RMIResourceManager` with an error like "RMIResourceManager is not abstract and does not override abstract method reserveResource(String)".
